Andy Burnham (left) and Volodymyr Zelensky during a recent visit to Portsmouth

Andy Burnham is marking his first foreign visit as prime minister with a trip to Kyiv - and will hand over blueprints so Ukraine can build its own long-range missiles.

The prime minister will chair his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.

He is also set to accept an award on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for Ukraine and to take part in independence day events.

Crucially for the war effort, he will announce his government has agreed to allow defence company MBDA to declassify information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile – the French equivalent of the UK's Storm Shadow.

Burnham will be reaffirming the UK's backing for Kyiv in the wake of escalating Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent weeks - including one on a shopping centre on Friday that killed at least 16 people.

Ahead of his visit on Monday, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.

"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."

He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

It comes after Moscow warned of "consequences" over the use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of strikes on Russian infrastructure.

Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries.

Watch: Burnham pledges support in first meeting with Zelensky

The Russian embassy in the UK has accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay".

In response, Burnham said last week: "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change."

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has agreed to provide Ukraine with blueprints to produce long-range missiles.

He is set to announce during his first trip to Ukraine that he will allow European defence firm MBDA to declassify information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile – the French-produced version of the UK's Storm Shadow.

The "deep precision strike" missiles use shared French and British technology, and Ukraine and France are looking to set up local assembly lines to produce them in Ukraine.

The prime minister is visiting Kyiv on his first foreign trip to mark Ukraine's independence day and signal the UK's continued support for the country under his administration.

He will arrive on Monday morning and is set to chair his first meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, set up by the UK and France to support Ukraine under his predecessor, Keir Starmer.

The prime minister will also take part in Independence Day events and accept an award on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support.

Burnham is set to assure Ukrainians of the UK's backing and reiterate that Russia's threats only strengthen British resolve.

Moscow recently threatened "consequences" over the reported use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of deep strikes into Russia's mainland.

Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.

"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."

Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to the UK during his first weeks in office.

The prime minister said: "The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia's illegal war. In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine and deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.

"Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

Last week, Russia accused the UK of deliberately escalating the conflict in relation to the UK-made drones and said the deeper the country's involvement became, "the higher the price it will pay".

Russia's ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, has left his post in London in recent weeks.
